Qur'anic verse: ﴿Ṭā Sīn Mīm﴾

We have discussed the disjointed letters (ḥurūf al-hijāʾ) at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. What is specific to this place is that it has been said: the ṭāʾ stands for dhū al-ṭawl (the Possessor of Bounty), the sīn stands for al-Samīʿ (the All-Hearing) or al-Salām (the Source of Peace), and the mīm stands for al-Raḥīm (the Most Merciful) or al-Munʿim (the Bestower of Favour).

﴿Consuming yourself﴾ is mentioned in [Surah] al-Kahf. ﴿Their necks would remain bowed before it﴾: "al-a'nāq" is the plural of "ʿunq" (neck), the well-known bodily part. The plural form "khāḍiʿīn" (bowed) is used in the masculine rational plural (ʿuqalāʾ, rational beings), because the necks are attributed to rational beings, and because it describes them with an action that only rational beings perform. It has also been said that "al-aʿnāq" means the chiefs of the people, who are compared to necks, just as they are called "heads" (ruʾūs) and "chests" (ṣudūr). It has also been said that it means groups of people, so the plural "khāḍiʿīn" needs no interpretation (taʾwīl, interpretive explanation).

﴿Recent (muḥdath)﴾ means the newness of its coming. ﴿So they will certainly receive it﴾ (the verse) is a threat. ﴿Of every kind (min kulli zawj)﴾ means of every type of plant, which includes foodstuffs, fruits, medicines and pasture. It is described as ﴿noble (karīm)﴾ because of the beauty and benefits it contains. ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: the demonstrative refers to the plants mentioned earlier. He used the singular form because He intended that in each one there is a sign, or it refers to the verbal noun of His statement ﴿We caused to grow (anbatnā)﴾.

﴿And my chest tightens﴾ is in the nominative (بالرفع, *bi-l-raf'*), coordinated with *akhaf* ("I fear"), or it is a new, independent sentence (*istinaf*, a resumed clause). It has also been read in the accusative (بالنصب, *bi-l-nasb*), coordinated with ﴿they deny me﴾ (يُكَذِّبُونِ).

﴿So send for Harun﴾: i.e., make him a messenger with me, to whom I may turn for help.

﴿And they have a charge against me﴾: i.e., his killing of the Copt.

﴿He said: "Never!"﴾: i.e., do not fear that they will kill you.

﴿Indeed, We are with you﴾: this is addressed to Musa, his brother, and those who were with them. Alternatively, the two are treated as a group (جماعة, *jama'ah*).

﴿Listeners﴾: its form (لفظه, *lafzuhu*) is plural (مُّسْتَمِعُونَ, *mustami'un*), and it occurs in the sense of exalting God, the Exalted. It is possible that the angels are the ones who hear by God's command, since God is not described as "listening" (الاستماع, *al-istima'*) but as "hearing" (السمع, *al-sam'*). The first view is better. Its explanation is that listening (الاستماع) carries an attentiveness and concern for the matter that is absent from the attribute of hearing (سامعون, *sami'un*).

The address in ﴿with you﴾ (مَعَكُمْ) is to Musa, Harun, Fir'awn and his people. It has also been said that it is to Musa and Harun alone, treating the two as a group, on the view of those who hold that the minimum of plurality is two.

﴿Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord﴾: If it is asked, "Why is it singular (رَسُولُ) when they are two?" the answer has three aspects.
First, the sense is: each one of us is a messenger.
Second, the two are treated as one person, because they agree in the sacred law (الشريعة, *al-shari'ah*), and because they are brothers, so they are as one.
Third, *rasul* here is a verbal noun (مصدر, *masdar*) used as a description, so it applies to the one, the two and the group alike, since it may be said *rasul* in the sense of *risalah* (mission). This differs from His saying ﴿innā rasūlā﴾ (إنا رسولا), where it means "messengers" (الرسل, *al-rusul*).

﴿That you send with us the Children of Israel﴾: i.e., release them.

﴿He said: "Did we not raise you among us as a child?"﴾: Fir'awn intended by these words to remind Musa of favour, as a way of belittling him.

Pharaoh said: ﴿Do you not listen?﴾, in astonishment at his answer. Moses increased the establishment of proof with His words ﴿your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾, because the existence of a human being and his forefathers is the clearest evidence among the intelligent and the greatest of proofs, for their own selves are the closest things to them, so they reason from them to the existence of their Creator. When this proof became manifest, Pharaoh deviated from it and attributed madness to Moses as a sophistry from himself, and he reinforced scorn and mockery in his words ﴿Your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾. Moses then increased the establishment of proof with His words ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾, because the rising and setting of the sun is a manifest sign that no one can deny, nor can anyone claim it for other than God. For this reason Abraham the Friend (al-Khalīl) established the proof by it against Nimrod. When Pharaoh was cut off by the proof, he returned to domination and dominance, and threatened him with prison. Moses then established the proof against him by the miracle, and mentioned it to him gently, hoping for his faith, saying: ﴿Even if I brought you something clear?﴾ The waw is a waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl) to which the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifhām) was attached, and its implied sense is: "Will you do that to me even if I bring you something clear?" The staff and the hand were mentioned earlier in al-Aʿrāf, and ﴿What do you command?﴾, ﴿Delay him﴾, and ﴿and gatherers﴾.

If it is asked: how did he first say ﴿if you are certain﴾, and then at the end say ﴿if you have intellect (taʿqilūn)﴾? The answer is that he softened (lāna) at first, hoping for their faith, and when he saw from them stubbornness and sophistry, he rebuked them with His words ﴿if you have intellect﴾, and he made this correspond to the words of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed your messenger ... is surely mad.﴾

﴿for the appointed time of a known day﴾: it is the day of the festival. ﴿We will follow the sorcerers﴾: that is, we will follow them in supporting our religion, not in practicing sorcery, because practicing sorcery was forbidden. ﴿By the might of Pharaoh﴾: an oath they swore. The explanation of ﴿what they were fabricating﴾ and what follows has already been given in Surat al-A'raf [7:117]. ﴿No harm﴾: that is, it will not harm us, because we will return to Allah. ﴿Travel by night with My servants﴾: meaning the Children of Israel. ﴿Indeed, you will be pursued﴾: a report that Pharaoh would pursue them. ﴿Indeed, these are a small band﴾: a shirdhima is a group of people. In this there is belittling of them, although it is narrated that they were six hundred thousand, but Pharaoh's soldiers were far more numerous than them. ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs﴾: meaning those in Egypt. The springs are the channels flowing out from the Nile, and there were springs at that time. It has also been said that it means gold and silver, but this is far-fetched. ﴿And noble dwellings﴾: the councils of rulers and governors. It has been said: the pulpits. It has also been said: the fine homes. ﴿Thus﴾: it is in the genitive position as an attribute of "dwelling," or in the accusative position with the sense: We expelled them in that same manner, or in the nominative position as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: the matter is thus. ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾: that is, Allah made them inherit the places of Pharaoh in Egypt. However, the histories do not mention that the Children of Israel ruled Egypt; what is known is that they ruled al-Sham (the Levant). So its interpretation according to this view is that He made them inherit the like of that in al-Sham. ﴿So they pursued them﴾: that is, they caught up with them. The subject pronoun refers to Pharaoh and his people, and the object pronoun refers to the Children of Israel. ﴿At sunrise﴾: its meaning is that they entered the time of sunrise, which is the rising of the sun. It has also been said: its meaning is toward the east, and it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

﴿When the two groups saw each other﴾. The word *tarā'ā* is on the pattern *tafā'ala*. It is in the accusative and derives from *al-ru'yah* (seeing). "The two groups" are the followers of Musa (Moses) and the followers of Fir'awn (Pharaoh). That is, each saw the other.

﴿Then it split﴾. The sentence implies its full form: Musa struck the sea, and so it split. ﴿Each part﴾ means each portion of it. *Al-ṭawd* is a mountain. It is narrated that twelve paths appeared in the sea, one path for each tribe (*sibt*) of the Children of Isra'il.

﴿And We brought the others near there﴾. "The others" means Fir'awn and his people. The meaning of *azlafnā* is that We brought them close to the sea so that they would drown. *Thamma* here is an adverb of place, meaning the place where the sea split. This is the Red Sea (*Bahr al-Qulzum*).

﴿What do you worship?﴾ He asked them this although He knew that they worshipped idols, in order to show them that what they worshipped was nothing, and to establish the proof against them.

﴿They said: "We worship idols"﴾. If it is asked why they stated explicitly "we worship", when the question "What do you worship?" would have been enough without an explicit answer: the parallel for such dispensing with an explicit answer through the indication of the question is His saying ﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾ [An-Nahl: 30], to which they replied ﴿Good﴾ [An-Nahl: 30]. The answer is that they stated it explicitly out of pride and delight in worshipping idols. Then they added ﴿so we remain devoted to them﴾ as an intensification of this.

﴿Rather, we found our fathers doing so﴾ is an acknowledgement of pure imitation (*taqlid*).

﴿Except the Lord of the worlds﴾. This is an exception of disconnection (*istithna' munqati'*). It was also said to be a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*), because among their forefathers were those who worshipped Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And when I fall ill, it is He who cures me﴾. He attributed the illness to himself and attributed the cure to Allah, out of good manners (*ta'addub*) with Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 26, verse 82–90:

﴿أَن يَغْفِرَ لِي خَطِيئَتِي﴾ It is said that he meant his three lies mentioned in the hadith: his saying concerning his wife Sarah, "She is my sister," and his saying, ﴿إِنِّي سَقِيمٌ﴾ [al-Saffat: 89] ("Indeed, I am sick"), and his saying, ﴿بَلْ فَعَلَهُ كَبِيرُهُمْ﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63] ("Rather, the biggest of them did it"). He meant the category in its absolute sense, because these three are ma'arid (indirect statements, or equivocations), and there is no sin in them. ﴿لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ﴾ means a good praise. ﴿يَوْمَ لاَ يَنفَعُ﴾ and what follows it is disconnected from the speech of Abraham and is from the speech of God Most High, though it may also be from the speech of Abraham: ﴿إِلاَّ مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾ ("except for one who comes to God with a sound heart"). It is said: sound from polytheism and sins. It is also said: one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. It is also said: with a heart stung (la'id) by fear of God, and the sound (salim) is in the language the one stung (la'id). Al-Zamakhshari said: this is among the strange (bida') interpretations. This exception may be connected (muttasil), so that ﴿مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ﴾ is the object of ﴿لاَ يَنفَعُ﴾. The meaning on this reading is that wealth does not benefit except for one who spends it in obedience to God, and that the prophets do not benefit except those whom they taught religion and enjoined the truth upon. It may also be connected, with ﴿مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ﴾ being a substitute (badal) for ﴿مَالٌ وَلاَ بَنُونَ﴾, with an omitted modifier, its meaning being: except the wealth of one who comes to God and his sons. It may also be disconnected (munqati'), in the sense of "but" (lakin). ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتِ ٱلْجَنَّةُ﴾ means it was brought near.

He meant the category in its absolute sense, because these three are ma'arid (indirect statements, or equivocations), and there is no sin in them. ﴿لِسَانَ صِدْقٍ﴾ means a good praise. ﴿يَوْمَ لاَ يَنفَعُ﴾ and what follows it is disconnected from the speech of Abraham and is from the speech of God Most High, though it may also be from the speech of Abraham: ﴿إِلاَّ مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾ ("except for one who comes to God with a sound heart"). It is said: sound from polytheism and sins. It is also said: one who meets his Lord with nothing in his heart other than Him. It is also said: with a heart stung (la'id) by fear of God, and the sound (salim) is in the language the one stung (la'id). Al-Zamakhshari said: this is among the strange (bida') interpretations. This exception may be connected (muttasil), so that ﴿مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ﴾ is the object of ﴿لاَ يَنفَعُ﴾. The meaning on this reading is that wealth does not benefit except for one who spends it in obedience to God, and that the prophets do not benefit except those whom they taught religion and enjoined the truth upon. It may also be connected, with ﴿مَنْ أَتَى ٱللَّهَ﴾ being a substitute (badal) for ﴿مَالٌ وَلاَ بَنُونَ﴾, with an omitted modifier, its meaning being: except the wealth of one who comes to God and his sons. It may also be disconnected (munqati'), in the sense of "but" (lakin). ﴿وَأُزْلِفَتِ ٱلْجَنَّةُ﴾ means it was brought near.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 26, verses 91–116:

﴿And Hellfire will be brought forward for the deviators.﴾ "The deviators" means the polytheists, as indicated by what follows. ﴿Then they will be thrown into it, they and the deviators,﴾ "kubkibu" is an intensive form of "kabba," whose letters are repeated to indicate the repetition of its meaning: that is, Allah throws them into the Fire again and again. The pronoun refers to the idols, and the deviators are the polytheists. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the deviators are the devils. ﴿When We made you equal with the Lord of the worlds.﴾ That is, We made you equal to Him. ﴿And none led us astray except the criminals.﴾ This means their great leaders, and the people of sin and audacity among them. ﴿Nor a close friend.﴾ "Hamim" means one whose affection is sincere. Al-Zamakhshari said: the plural "intercessors" is used but the singular "friend" is used, because intercessors are usually numerous while friends are few. ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ The verb is attributed to "the people," and it carries the feminine marker, because "qawm" means a group and a nation. If it is asked: how does He say "the messengers" in the plural when they denied only Noah alone? The answer is in two respects. First, he intended the category, as when you say: "So-and-so rides horses," though he rode only one horse. Second, whoever denies one prophet has denied all the prophets, peace be upon them, because their message is one and their call is the same. The same answer applies to: ﴿ʿĀd denied the messengers﴾ and others. ﴿And the lowly ones have followed you.﴾ The plural of "arhal" (lowly, base), which was discussed in His words ﴿"our lowly ones"﴾ in Hud [27]. ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers.﴾ That is, those whom they called lowly. The disbelievers wanted Noah to drive them away, just as the Quraysh wanted the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to drive away ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Suhayb, Bilal and others like them among the weak. ﴿Among the stoned.﴾ This may mean they intend stoning with stones, or stoning with words, which is insult.

It is also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the deviators are the devils. ﴿When We made you equal with the Lord of the worlds.﴾ That is, We made you equal to Him. ﴿And none led us astray except the criminals.﴾ This means their great leaders, and the people of sin and audacity among them. ﴿Nor a close friend.﴾ "Hamim" means one whose affection is sincere. Al-Zamakhshari said: the plural "intercessors" is used but the singular "friend" is used, because intercessors are usually numerous while friends are few. ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers.﴾ The verb is attributed to "the people," and it carries the feminine marker, because "qawm" means a group and a nation. If it is asked: how does He say "the messengers" in the plural when they denied only Noah alone? The answer is in two respects. First, he intended the category, as when you say: "So-and-so rides horses," though he rode only one horse. ﴿The custom of the ancients﴾ is read with a *ḍamma* on the *khā'* and the *lām* (*khuluq*), meaning their habit. The meaning is that they said: "This religion you are upon is nothing but the custom of the earlier people." Ibn Kathir, al-Kasa'i and Abu 'Amr read it with a *fatḥa* on the *khā'* and a *sukūn* on the *lām* (*khalq*). On this reading there are two possibilities. The first is that it means creation (*khilqah*), so the meaning is: "This form we are upon is nothing but the form of the earlier people." The second is that it derives from *ikhtilāq* (fabrication), meaning falsehood, so the meaning is: "What you have brought is nothing but the lies of the earlier people."

﴿Will you be left﴾: this is a warning to them. Its meaning is: do you expect to be left in blessings despite your disbelief?

﴿And date palms whose spathes are delicate﴾: the *ṭal'* is the cluster of dates at the beginning of its growth, before it emerges from its sheath. It is also possible that He meant gardens that contain no date palms, and then He joined the date palms to them with a conjunction.

It was also said to mean strong, or insolent and arrogant. ﴿Min al-musaḥḥarīn (among the bewitched)﴾ is an intensive form of al-masḥūrīn (those who are bewitched). It comes from siḥr with a kasra on the sin. It was also said to come from siḥr with a fatḥa on the sin, meaning sight. On this reading the meaning is: ﴿you are only a human being like us﴾.

﴿Mimmā ya'malūn (from what they do)﴾ means: deliver me from the punishment for their deeds, or protect me from their deeds. The first is more preferred.

﴿Min al-mukhsirīn (among those who give less)﴾ means among those who cheat in measure and weight. ﴿Bil-qisṭās (with the balance)﴾ means the upright balance. ﴿Wal-jibillah (and the former generations)﴾ means the earlier generations. ﴿ʿAdhābu yawm al-ẓullah (the punishment of the Day of the Shade)﴾: it was a cloud of fire that burned them. **Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 26, verses 192–212**

﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit﴾ means Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. ﴿Upon your heart﴾ indicates his memorising it, because the heart is what retains. ﴿In clear Arabic language﴾ means the speech of the Arabs. The phrase ﴿in clear Arabic language﴾ is connected either to "descended" or to "the warners." ﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the earlier peoples﴾: the meaning is that the Qur'an is mentioned in the books of the earlier ones, and this is evidence for its authenticity. Then he established the proof against Quraysh by his saying: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that it is known by the scholars of the Children of Israel?﴾, meaning that it is from Allah, a sign and a proof for you. The intended ones are those among the Children of Israel who embraced Islam, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam. It is also said that they are those who used to give glad tidings of his (ﷺ) mission.

﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs...﴾: the word is the plural of aʿjam, which means one who does not speak, whether a human, an animal or an inanimate thing. The aʿjamī is one attributed to the ʿajam (non-Arabs), i.e., other than Arabs [. . .]. It is also said that it means the same as aʿjam. The meaning of the verse is that if the Qur'an had been sent down to someone who could not speak, and then he recited it to them, they would not have believed, because of the extremity of their obstinacy. In this there is consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding their disbelief despite the clarity of its proof.

﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ The meaning of ﴿We caused it to enter﴾ is: We made it enter. The pronoun refers to the denial that is indicated by what preceded in the speech, or to the Qur'an; that is, We caused it to enter their hearts as a denier of it. The sense of ﴿thus﴾ is: like this inserting, We inserted it. The ﴿criminals﴾ may refer to Quraysh or to earlier disbelievers. ﴿They will not believe﴾ is an explanation of the insertion which He made into their hearts.

﴿So that they will say, "Will we be reprieved?"﴾: they wish to be delayed when wishing will not benefit them.

﴿Then is it Our punishment they seek to hasten?﴾ This is a rebuke to Quraysh for their seeking to hasten the punishment in their saying: ﴿"Throw down your staff"﴾ [an-Naml: 10], and ﴿"Rain down upon us stones from the sky"﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], and what is similar to that.

﴿Have you considered if We let them enjoy for years...﴾: the meaning is that the duration of their being given respite does not avail them once the punishment descends after it, even if the period extends for years, because everything that is coming is near. Some have said: ﴿years﴾ means the lifespan of the world.

﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners﴾: the meaning is that Allah did not destroy a people except after establishing the proof against them by sending to them a messenger who warned them, and they denied him. ﴿A reminder﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun from the sense of "warning," or in the accusative as a circumstantial state from the pronoun in "warners," or in the accusative as an object of purpose, or in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject.

﴿And the devils did not bring it down﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and this is a refutation of those who said it is soothsaying which the devils brought down upon Muhammad. ﴿It is not befitting for them, nor are they able﴾: that is, it is not possible for them and they are not capable of it. The expression ﴿it is not befitting﴾ is sometimes used in the sense of "it is not possible" and sometimes in the sense of "it is not appropriate."

﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing [the heavenly speech]﴾: this is a reason for the devils' inability to practise soothsaying, because they were prevented from eavesdropping since the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), whereas the matter of soothsayers (kahana, soothsaying) had been widespread and common before that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 26, verse 214–223:

﴿And warn your closest kinsmen.﴾ The ʿashīra (clan, close kin) of a man are his nearest relatives. Then he likewise called out to his daughter Fatimah and his aunt Safiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: In its meaning there are two opinions. One is that he was commanded to begin by warning his close relatives before other people. The other is that he was commanded not to be swayed by the tenderness a close relative feels for his kin, and not to hold back from warning them out of fear of them.
﴿And lower your wing﴾ is an expression for gentleness of disposition, kindness, and humility.
﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ means when you stand in prayer, though it may also mean all your movements.
﴿And your turning about among those who prostrate﴾ is coordinated with the object pronoun in His saying "who sees you," and the meaning is that He sees you when you stand and when you prostrate. It was also said: the meaning is that He sees your prayer together with those who pray, and in this there is an indication of congregational prayer. It was also said: He sees the turning of your gaze among those who pray behind you, for the Prophet ﷺ used to see them from behind his back.
﴿The angels descend upon every sinful liar﴾ is the answer to the previous question, which is His saying: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ The "afak" is the liar, and the "athim" is the one who commits sin; by this is meant the soothsayers (kuhhan). ﴿They give ear﴾ means they listen. The pronoun may refer to the devils, meaning they listen to the angels, or to the soothsayers, meaning they listen to the devils. It was also said: ﴿yulqun﴾ means they convey what is heard, and the pronoun on this view may also refer to the devils, because they convey speech to the soothsayers, or to the soothsayers, because they convey speech to people.
﴿And most of them are liars﴾ means the devils or the soothsayers, because they lie in what they report about the devils.

When this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ warned his kinsmen, saying: "O Banu Hashim, save yourselves from the Fire! O Banu ʿAbd al-Muttalib, save yourselves from the Fire!" Then he likewise called out to his daughter Fatimah and his aunt Safiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: In its meaning there are two opinions. One is that he was commanded to begin by warning his close relatives before other people. The other is that he was commanded not to be swayed by the tenderness a close relative feels for his kin, and not to hold back from warning them out of fear of them.
﴿And lower your wing﴾ is an expression for gentleness of disposition, kindness, and humility.
﴿Who sees you when you stand﴾ means when you stand in prayer, though it may also mean all your movements.
﴿And your turning about among those who prostrate﴾ is coordinated with the object pronoun in His saying "who sees you," and the meaning is that He sees you when you stand and when you prostrate. It was also said: the meaning is that He sees your prayer together with those who pray, and in this there is an indication of congregational prayer. It was also said: He sees the turning of your gaze among those who pray behind you, for the Prophet ﷺ used to see them from behind his back.
﴿The angels descend upon every sinful liar﴾ is the answer to the previous question, which is His saying: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ The "afak" is the liar, and the "athim" is the one who commits sin; by this is meant the soothsayers (kuhhan). In this is a refutation of those who claim that the devils descended upon our master Muhammad ﷺ with soothsaying, for they descend only upon a sinful liar, while he ﷺ was at the utmost degree of truthfulness and piety.
﴿They give ear﴾ means they listen. The pronoun may refer to the devils, meaning they listen to the angels, or to the soothsayers, meaning they listen to the devils. It was also said: ﴿yulqun﴾ means they convey what is heard, and the pronoun on this view may also refer to the devils, because they convey speech to the soothsayers, or to the soothsayers, because they convey speech to people.
﴿And most of them are liars﴾ means the devils or the soothsayers, because they lie in what they report about the devils.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 26, verses 224–227:

﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them.﴾ Having mentioned the soothsayers (kuhhan), he mentioned the poets (shu'ara') to make clear that the Qur'an is neither soothsaying nor poetry, because of the difference between its attributes and the attributes of poetry and soothsaying. He meant the poets who utter from poetry what is not fitting, such as satire (hija'), false praise (madh bil-batil), and other things. It was also said: he meant the poets of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic era). It was also said: the poets of the disbelieving Quraysh who used to harm the Muslims with their verses. As for the deviators (al-ghawun), it was said: they are the transmitters of poetry (ruwat al-shi'r). It was said: they are the foolish among people, whom poems please because of what they contain of vain and falsehood. It was also said: they are the devils.

﴿In every valley they wander.﴾ This is a metaphor and an image (isti'ara wa tamthil), meaning: they go off in every direction of speech, true and false, and they exceed bounds in figurative language (tajawwuz) until they arrive at falsehood.

﴿Except those who believe﴾ — the verse is an exception from the poets, meaning by them the poets of the Muslims, such as Hassan ibn Thabit and others who were characterized by these attributes. It was also said that this verse is Medinan.

﴿And they remember Allah much﴾ — it was said: its meaning is that they remembered Allah in their poetry. It was also said: it means remembrance in its general sense.

﴿And they defend themselves after they have been wronged﴾ — an allusion to what Hassan ibn Thabit and other poets said in satirizing the disbelievers after the disbelievers had satirized the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿And those who have wronged will know what [sort of] return they will be returned to﴾ — a warning to those who wronged. The wrong (zulm) here means aggression against people, based on His saying: ﴿after they have been wronged﴾. The verb yanqalibun governs ayya because of its position (ta'akhkhuruhu); and it was said: the governing element of ayya is sa-ya'lamu (will know).
